markPoints.concept: sending a message pretending to be someone trustworthy, to get personal information
markPoints.exemplar: Sending a message that pretends to be from a trusted company, to get somebody's password.

questions.example: Sending an email or message that pretends to be from a trusted organisation, so that the victim gives away personal information such as a password or bank details.
questions.paraphrase: Contacting someone while posing as a company they trust, in order to trick them into handing over their login details.
questions.feedback: Pretending to be trusted, in order to get something. Both halves.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.4 Lesson 4 — Phishing inbox, station 1: What is phishing?

questions.q: Which of these are signs that an email may be phishing? Tick all that apply.
options: The sender's address does not match the organisation it claims to be from
It creates urgency, such as threatening to close an account
The link goes to an address that is not the company's own
It asks for a password or bank details
It is addressed to the recipient by name
correct: The sender's address does not match the organisation it claims to be from
It creates urgency, such as threatening to close an account
The link goes to an address that is not the company's own
It asks for a password or bank details
questions.feedback: Being addressed by name is not a sign of safety: spear phishing does exactly that, using information from social media.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.4 Lesson 4 — Phishing inbox, station 1: What is phishing?

questions.q: Explain why spear phishing is more likely to succeed than ordinary phishing.

markPoints.concept: it is aimed at one person and uses details about them
accept: one person|an individual|a single person|specific|targeted|directed at|particular person|named|personal details|their name|about them|about their|researched
markPoints.exemplar: It is aimed at one particular person and uses real details about them.

markPoints.concept: so it looks far more convincing and the usual warning signs are missing
accept: convincing|believable|realistic|genuine|authentic|trustworthy|credible|harder to spot|looks real|looks like it|warning signs|no signs|clues|less suspicious|nothing obvious
markPoints.exemplar: This makes it far more convincing, so the victim is less likely to be suspicious.

questions.example: Spear phishing targets one individual and uses real details about them, often taken from social media, so the message looks like it genuinely comes from someone who knows them and the usual warning signs are not there.
questions.paraphrase: Because it is directed at a single person and draws on information about their life, the message appears authentic and the normal clues that something is wrong are absent.
